title: Replace combinational division with an iterative shared divider
motivation:
The baseline's 199.837 ns worst path passes through the execute ALU and has
156 logic cells. The ALU currently infers four independent 32-bit divide and
remainder expressions, including signed and unsigned variants. Their large
combinational networks dominate timing and inflate LUT use even though the
pipeline executes at most one M-extension operation at a time.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline's 199.837 ns worst path passes through the execute ALU and has
156 logic cells. The ALU currently infers four independent 32-bit divide and
remainder expressions, including signed and unsigned variants. Their large
combinational networks dominate timing and inflate LUT use even though the
pipeline executes at most one M-extension operation at a time.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Use one 32-cycle radix-2 unsigned quotient/remainder engine for DIV, DIVU,
REM, and REMU, with operand magnitude conversion and result sign correction
for signed operations. Latch the operands and operation when a division
enters EX. Hold PC and ID/EX while it runs; let the older EX/MEM operation
advance once into MEM/WB, then inject EX/MEM bubbles until the divide result
is ready. Existing dmem backpressure retains priority so an older memory
request is held until acknowledged, never issued twice.
Preserve divide-by-zero and INT_MIN/-1 results exactly. Keep the existing
RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitutions and avoid starting the real divider in
that configuration. This removes the long combinational divide paths from
the clock period; the extra cycles should be outweighed by a substantial
Fmax increase on CoreMark, where division is a minority of instructions.

Exercise the new divide start/ready handshake with exact RV32M bit results, including back-to-back, signed, unsigned, zero-divisor, and overflow cases.

title: Replace combinational division with an iterative M unit
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz and uses 12,312 LUT4s. Its 156-cell
critical path runs through forwarding, EX, and the ALU to a memory output.
The four 32-bit combinational divide and remainder operators are the most
likely source of both the deep arithmetic path and excess LUT use. CoreMark
executes many ordinary ALU and memory operations between divisions, so a
longer divider latency can be repaid by a substantially shorter clock.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz and uses 12,312 LUT4s. Its 156-cell
critical path runs through forwarding, EX, and the ALU to a memory output.
The four 32-bit combinational divide and remainder operators are the most
likely source of both the deep arithmetic path and excess LUT use. CoreMark
executes many ordinary ALU and memory operations between divisions, so a

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU with one shared, eight-cycle radix-16
restoring divider that resolves four quotient bits per EX cycle
inside the existing ALU source, which the fixed formal source list includes.
Latch the forwarded operands and operation when a valid divide starts;
use signed-magnitude conversion and result correction for signed operations,
with explicit divide-by-zero and INT_MIN/-1 behavior. While the divider is
busy, hold PC and ID/EX, inject bubbles into EX/MEM so older instructions
drain exactly once, and suppress branch redirects from any held instruction.
Release the pipeline only when the result is captured into EX/MEM, including
if a dmem stall outlasts the calculation. Keep all non-division operations at
their present single-cycle EX latency. Perform the first quotient step on
launch and capture the final result on the eighth EX cycle so an isolated
divide stays within the unchanged bounded formal liveness window. Retain the
RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS arithmetic substitution for the formal configuration.
This should remove the divider from the clock's critical combinational path,
reduce LUT count, and improve CoreMark iterations per second despite the
extra cycles on division instructions.

Interlock fetch and decode for a divide while allowing older instructions to drain and giving dmem stalls and redirects correct priority.
Connect the EX divider interlock and update pipeline control so divide instructions retire once in order under independent imem and dmem stalls.
Adapt the existing RV32M vectors to the ALU handshake, preserving every divide/remainder check and testing consecutive operations and result retention under a consumer stall.

title: Fetch-stage bimodal branch prediction
motivation:
The bench core always fetches PC+4 and resolves branches in EX. Every taken
branch therefore discards the younger fetched instruction. CoreMark contains
repeated loops, so avoiding these redirects should raise iterations per
cycle without changing the divider-dominated critical path.

hypothesis.motivation:
The bench core always fetches PC+4 and resolves branches in EX. Every taken
branch therefore discards the younger fetched instruction. CoreMark contains
repeated loops, so avoiding these redirects should raise iterations per
cycle without changing the divider-dominated critical path.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 64-entry, two-bit saturating direction table indexed by branch PC.
At IF, decode the fetched instruction just enough to recognize legal
conditional branches and JAL, form their immediate target, and select the
next fetch PC. Predict conditional branches from the table (initially weak
not-taken); predict aligned JAL targets unconditionally. Carry that predicted
next PC with the instruction through ID/EX. EX still computes the true next
PC, including misalignment traps, and redirects and flushes only when the
predicted next PC differs. Train the table once when a valid legal branch
advances from EX; never train a held or annulled instruction. JALR continues
to resolve in EX. On imem or dmem backpressure, preserve the current PC and
prediction metadata so no fetched instruction is lost or retired twice.
The smaller misprediction rate should improve CoreMark IPC enough to exceed
the 4.6 percent acceptance margin while adding modest FPGA storage.

title: Keep bubble control off the wide fetch and decode data paths
motivation:
The 32-cycle divider raised Fmax to 43.953 MHz, but the new 42-cell worst
path runs from forwarding through EX branch resolution, fetch flushing,
hazard control, and the ID/EX operand register. A nearly equal path ends
at the PC register through the same fetch/hazard detour. Redirect currently
replaces the whole fetched instruction with a NOP, and ID flush clears the
entire ID/EX bundle. Thus branch control reaches wide data and register-input
muxes even though a killed instruction only needs its side effects disabled.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Represent fetch and decode bubbles with valid and zeroed control bits,
leaving instruction and operand payload outside the redirect/flush muxes.
Have IF pass imem_data directly and mark a fetch invalid only when the
instruction bus is stalled. The existing ID flush kills the wrong-path
instruction on redirect, so redirect need not affect IF instruction or
validity. In ID, capture payload on ordinary unstalled cycles regardless
of validity, but clear ctrl and valid when either IF is invalid or ID is
flushed; on load-use flush clear only ctrl and valid while payload holds.
Gate load-use detection with imem_ready so arbitrary imem data during a
bus stall cannot create a false hazard. Invalid ID/EX entries must have
zero side-effect controls, including branch, memory, register write, and
divide selection. This removes the redirect-to-fetch-to-hazard detour from
both the PC and ID operand-register paths, shortening the clock period
without adding retirement cycles or changing any architectural result.

title: Register the fetch-to-decode boundary and squash by validity
motivation:
The current 43.953 MHz champion has a 42-cell, 27.48 ns critical path
from MEM-stage forwarding through EX branch resolution, IF redirect and
hazard control, then into the ID/EX operand register. IF currently passes
the instruction bus directly into decode and replaces a squashed instruction
with a NOP through a 32-bit mux. A branch decision therefore propagates
through decode and register-file read before reaching the next register.
The previous four-step divider regressed because it lengthened the EX path;
this proposal keeps the existing one-step-per-cycle divider intact.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Insert a registered, one-entry IF/ID instruction-and-PC buffer with an
explicit valid bit, turning IF and ID into separate pipeline stages. Fetch
enters the buffer only when io_imemReady is high; a missing response leaves
it empty, while downstream dmem or divide backpressure holds its contents.
On an EX redirect, synchronously invalidate both the buffered younger
instruction and the ID/EX instruction, and set the fetch PC to the target.
Do not send a NOP instruction through decode to squash: use validity to
prevent decode, regfile data, and control from affecting a killed entry.
Give redirect priority over stalls and ensure each accepted fetch reaches
ID exactly once. The extra register boundary should break the measured
forwarding-to-decode timing path and improve Fmax enough to outweigh the
additional taken-branch bubble; it may also retain a fetched instruction
through independent dmem backpressure instead of discarding it.

title: Compact timing-aware bimodal branch prediction
motivation:
The current iterative-divider core reaches 43.953 MHz, but its worst path
runs through EX branch resolution, the fetch PC, hazard control, and ID.
Its fetch stage always selects PC+4, so taken CoreMark branches inject
bubbles. A prior 64-entry bimodal predictor reduced cycles from 4,491,817
to 4,201,766, but that experiment used the old combinational-divider
circuit and ran at only 5.233 MHz. On the reference CoreMark trace, a
32-entry two-bit table makes about 55,556 conditional-branch mistakes,
only 3,710 more than a 64-entry table, compared with 111,175 for
backward-branch prediction. The smaller lookup and a shorter correction
path should help retain the current clock speed.

hypothesis.motivation:
The current iterative-divider core reaches 43.953 MHz, but its worst path
runs through EX branch resolution, the fetch PC, hazard control, and ID.
Its fetch stage always selects PC+4, so taken CoreMark branches inject
bubbles. A prior 64-entry bimodal predictor reduced cycles from 4,491,817
to 4,201,766, but that experiment used the old combinational-divider

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 32-entry, two-bit saturating direction table indexed by branch PC,
initialized weakly not taken. In IF, predict only validated conditional
branch encodings, and only when their computed target is aligned; predict
aligned JAL taken. Compute PC+4 and the branch/JAL target in IF, then carry
these addresses and one predicted-taken bit into ID/EX. EX detects a
conditional-branch miss by comparing the resolved taken bit with that bit;
it redirects to the precomputed fall-through or target and kills only the
younger wrong-path instruction. JALR remains resolved in EX and corrects
the sequential prediction when its aligned target differs. Train the
direction table exactly once when a valid legal branch advances from EX,
never while EX is held or the instruction is annulled. Keep the table write
registered, outside the current-cycle fetch steering path.
This keeps target addition and a 32-bit predicted-PC comparator out of the
forwarding-to-PC correction cone. Keep prediction metadata aligned with
its instruction through imem, dmem, load-use, and divider stalls; preserve
misaligned target traps, RVFI PC fields, and the iterative RV32M divider.
Reducing loop-branch bubbles while holding or improving Fmax should clear
the 4.6 percent champion margin.

title: Dedicated effective-address path for loads and stores
motivation:
The current champion retires ten CoreMark iterations in 4,203,461 cycles at
49.114 MHz. Its 15-cell worst path starts in the register file, crosses ID
and the EX ALU, and ends at data memory. Loads and stores currently form
their address through the general ALU's operand selection and result case
mux, even though every legal memory operation needs only rs1 plus a signed
immediate. A previous timing-only simplification reached 51.546 MHz, so
shortening this active address path is large enough to plausibly clear
the 4.6 percent acceptance margin without changing instruction timing.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Compute the load/store effective address with a dedicated 32-bit adder fed
directly by the forwarded rs1 value and the decoded immediate. Register
that sum in EX/MEM as the memory address and route the MEM-stage address,
byte-lane selection, alignment check, and RVFI memory address from it.
Keep the general ALU for arithmetic, jumps, and M-extension operations;
memory instructions need no result from its operation mux. Avoid placing
the memory-op selection after the dedicated adder on the data-memory
address path. This trades a small amount of adder/register area for fewer
LUT levels on the measured critical path, with no new pipeline stalls.
Preserve forwarded operands, load/store alignment traps, bus backpressure,
and the exact RVFI memory fields.

title: Separate load-store address generation from the execute ALU
motivation:
The current champion's 27.265 ns worst path starts at the register file,
crosses decode, forwarding, and the execute ALU, and ends at a data-memory
output. Loads and stores use the general ALU's 19-operation result mux merely
to add rs1 and an immediate before driving the data-memory address. This
shared path is now more costly than branch prediction misses or division
latency, and improving it requires no extra instruction cycles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split effective-address generation from the general execute ALU. In EX,
compute load/store addresses with a dedicated 32-bit rs1-plus-immediate
adder fed by the existing forwarded rs1 operand. Register this address in
its own EX/MEM field and drive the data-memory address, alignment checks,
byte selection, and RVFI memory address from that field. Keep the general
ALU result for register-writing arithmetic and jump links; a load uses its
memory result at WB and a store writes no register, so neither needs to
select the general ALU result on the memory address path. Preserve the
current stage count, predictor, divider handshake, stall priorities, and
single-channel retirement contract. This should shorten the measured
register-file-to-data-memory cone without increasing CoreMark cycles,
lifting Fmax by more than the 4.6 percent champion acceptance margin.
